precepts.text: To succeed in the name of the dead brother means the child inherits the dead man's possession and land so his name is not put out of Israel; a brother who refuses has his shoe loosed and his face spat in, and his house is named for it forever, because he would not love his neighbor as himself.
precepts.point: She bore twins; Zarah put out his hand first and got the scarlet thread, then drew it back and Pharez broke forth, so Pharez means a breach and the line of the kings runs through him.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
About three months after Judah went in to Tamar, she began to show, and word came to Judah that his daughter-in-law had played the harlot and was with child by whoredom. Her husband was dead and she was living in her father's house, so Judah said, “Bring her forth, and let her be burnt”: that was the law for a harlot. But she sent him his own signet, bracelets and staff, and “Judah acknowledged them, and said, She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son.” The child was his, and he was the one in the wrong.

Deuteronomy 25 shows what Judah and Onan owed her. Moses recites this law later, but our forefathers already had knowledge of it through oral tradition passed down from Adam. “If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her.” That is why it was wrong when Onan spilled his seed on the ground.

“the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.” To succeed in the name of the dead brother does not mean the child takes his actual name. It means the child inherits the dead man's possession, his land and his things, because he left no seed to inherit for him. The brother raises up a surrogate seed in honor of his dead brother, so the land stays in his brother's name and is not lost.

A brother who refuses is brought before the elders. His brother's wife shall “loose his shoe from off his foot, and spit in his face”, saying, “So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother’s house.” And “his name shall be called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.” He carries that humiliation forever, because he would not love his neighbor as himself. That is why the history of Ruth is so important. It is not about Ruth, the Moabite heathen woman; y'all make it about her because y'all love heathens.

So Tamar was more righteous than Judah: she kept her dead husband's name alive when Judah withheld Shelah. From her came twins. Zarah put out his hand first and the midwife bound a scarlet thread on it, but he drew it back and his brother broke forth: “this breach be upon thee: therefore his name was called Pharez.” Pharez means a breach, and the line of the kings runs through him.

precepts.text: A just weight and balance are the Lord's; all the weights of the bag are his work. Deal justly and you are in the spirit.
precepts.point: The other side of the promise is that an unjust balance shortens your days. One day somebody realizes you have been robbing them, and men kill over a dollar. The Lord wrote that from the beginning.

note.label: Covetous Eyes Will Be Put Out

precepts.why:
“But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have.” The Lord does not like people who are crooked. If you are going to do business, make sure you have a just balance; do not play with the scale and tilt it in your favor.

Solomon shows whose scale it is: “A just weight and balance are the Lord’s: all the weights of the bag are his work.” The just weight belongs to the Lord. So if you are dealing with a just weight and balance, you are in the spirit, and the Most High loves that.

The Most High is not a joke. He gives commandments on what you should do to live, and says keep them so that you may have life. Dealing justly with your brother is love, and “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.” Doing back-dealing with your brother shows no love; that is hatred. By being covetous you break many laws.

That is why the just weight comes with a promise: “that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.” The scale that is the Lord's is the scale that lengthens your days.

precepts.text: Divers weights and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the Lord. Crooked dealing makes the Lord look at you as an abomination.
precepts.point: The other side of the promise is that an unjust balance shortens your days. One day somebody realizes you have been robbing them, and men kill over a dollar. The Lord wrote that from the beginning.

note.label: Covetous Eyes Will Be Put Out

precepts.why:
“Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the Lord.” The great and the small that Deuteronomy forbids in the bag and in the house are both alike. If you are not doing the right dealings in your business, the Lord is looking at you as an abomination.

Eventually he is going to put your lights out, because he already warned you. If you want long life, have a just weight; that is the thing he is pleased in. If you have divers weights and divers measures, the Lord is not pleased, and your days are going to be short.

That is the other side of Deuteronomy 25:15. If a just weight lengthens your days, an unjust balance shortens them. One day somebody is going to realize you have been robbing them, and they are going to kill you. Dudes will kill you for a dollar; you would be surprised what people do. The Bible knows that, and the Lord wrote about it from the very beginning.

Had you been doing your four chapters a day and applying yourself, you would remember scriptures like this, and when the devil tried to tempt you, you would say no: the Bible says the Lord counts it an abomination.

precepts.text: Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant, but he knoweth not that the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell.
precepts.point: The other side of the promise is that an unjust balance shortens your days. One day somebody realizes you have been robbing them, and men kill over a dollar. The Lord wrote that from the beginning.

note.label: Covetous Eyes Will Be Put Out

precepts.why:
“Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant.” You feel good when you make that extra money from tilting the scale, when you are stealing. It tastes sweet.

“But he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell.” What he does not know is where it leads: death and condemnation. The one who eats the stolen bread is sitting among the dead.

So do not be a thief. Deal righteously; deal according to the law, statutes and commandments. The divers weights of Deuteronomy 25 are stolen waters, and the days they seem to add are really shortened, just as the law warned: the just weight is “that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.”

And pride keeps a man from hearing it: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.” Once people have a little money in their pocket, they feel grown and will not seek counsel, and when everything falls apart, then they want counsel. The scriptures say blessed is he that readeth; if we apply what we read, we will be all right.

precepts.text: The brother's duty to raise up a name in Israel became law, and the refuser bore public reproach; Onan refused that duty.
precepts.point: The sin was refusing to raise up seed to his brother, not the act itself; do not build a doctrine on the wrong point. What happened here later became law: the husband's brother raises up the name of the dead, and he that refuses has his shoe loosed and his face spat in, and his house carries the reproach.

note.label: Genesis 38: Judah and Tamar

precepts.why:
What happened with Onan later became law in Israel. “If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband’s brother unto her.” The firstborn she bears “shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.” That is exactly what Judah told Onan to do: go in unto thy brother’s wife, and raise up seed to thy brother.

The law also shows what the refuser is. If the man will not take her, she goes up to the gate unto the elders and says “My husband’s brother refuseth to raise up unto his brother a name in Israel”; and if he stands to it, she looses his shoe from off his foot, spits in his face, and says “So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother’s house.” Public reproach, and his house carries it.

So the sin of Onan was refusing to raise up seed to his brother, not the act itself. He knew the seed should not be his, and he spilled it on the ground “lest that he should give seed to his brother.” Do not build a doctrine on the wrong point: the thing that displeased the Lord, wherefore he slew him also, was refusing the duty of an husband’s brother.

precepts.text: Remember what Amalek did, how he smote the hindmost, the feeble, the faint and weary, and feared not God; thou shalt blot out his remembrance.
precepts.point: The enmity was set from the garden between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed. They bruised Christ's heel, but at the end of the world Jacob bruises the head: the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.

note.label: Exodus 17: Water Out of the Rock and War With Amalek

precepts.why:
“Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua”. Moses wrote it, and Deuteronomy 25 is that rehearsal: “Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt; How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.”

Amalek did not meet the mighty men in the front. He went to the back, to smite the hindmost, all that were feeble, when Israel was faint and weary: the women, the children and the old ones. And he feared not God. That same spirit works against the nation's young and old today.

“Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.” That is the “I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven” of Exodus, rehearsed forty years later. By then the children of Amalek had done nothing themselves, and the charge still stood: the judgment carries to the seed.

precepts.text: Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes save one; Paul recounted how he was beaten.
precepts.point: Forty stripes may he give him, and not exceed, lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee. Paul recounted receiving that beating under this law.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
The wicked man worthy to be beaten was made to lie down and be beaten before the judge's face, according to his fault, by a certain number. “Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.”

Paul recounted receiving that beating under this law: “Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes save one. Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep”. Forty stripes save one, five times, of the Jews: the beating by a certain number, not exceeding forty, that this law sets.

precepts.text: The elders that labour in the word and doctrine are worthy of double honour, for thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn.
precepts.point: Giving double honour is not just saying the words to the leadership; it is true respect and reverence toward the leadership that labours in this word and doctrine.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
“Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn”: the corn is the reward for the ox. Paul applies this verse to how the elders are treated: “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine. For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.”

The ox that treads out the corn is not kept from it; the elder that labours in the word and doctrine is worthy of his reward, double honour. Giving double honour is not just saying the words to the leadership; it is true respect and reverence toward the leadership that labours in this word and doctrine.

precepts.text: Onan refused to raise up seed to his brother Er, and the thing which he did displeased the Lord.
precepts.point: The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
Judah's house shows the duty of the husband's brother. “And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, whose name was Tamar. And Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord; and the Lord slew him. And Judah said unto Onan, Go in unto thy brother’s wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother.” That is the duty of this law: the husband's brother goes in unto her and raises up seed in the name of the dead.

“And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother’s wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother. And the thing which he did displeased the Lord: wherefore he slew him also.” Onan refused to raise up seed to his brother Er, and the thing which he did displeased the Lord, and the Lord slew him too.

precepts.text: Boaz answered Ruth that he would perform the kinsman's part, but there was a kinsman nearer than he.
precepts.point: The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
Ruth's husband was dead, and Boaz was a near kinsman. “And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I. Tarry this night, and it shall be in the morning, that if he will perform unto thee the part of a kinsman, well; let him do the kinsman’s part: but if he will not do the part of a kinsman to thee, then will I do the part of a kinsman to thee, as the Lord liveth”.

Boaz answered Ruth that he would perform the kinsman's part, but there was a kinsman nearer than he. The part of a kinsman is the duty of the husband's brother in this law: take the wife of the dead and raise up his name. Boaz blessed her for seeking it, “inasmuch as thou followedst not young men, whether poor or rich”, and all the city knew she was a virtuous woman.

precepts.text: The nearer kinsman could not redeem it, lest he mar his own inheritance, and the right passed to Boaz.
precepts.point: The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
Boaz went up to the gate, where this law sends the matter, and “took ten men of the elders of the city”. He said to the nearer kinsman: “Naomi, that is come again out of the country of Moab, selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech’s”, and “If thou wilt redeem it, redeem it”. The kinsman said, “I will redeem it.”

“Then said Boaz, What day thou buyest the field of the hand of Naomi, thou must buy it also of Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. And the kinsman said, I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance: redeem thou my right to thyself; for I cannot redeem it.” The nearer kinsman could not redeem it, lest he mar his own inheritance, and the right passed to Boaz.

Here is what the law stood for: raising up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. The name was not to be put out of Israel because of the land inheritance, and the wife of the dead and the field went together. Check this out: this is no longer the law, so do not try to use it as an excuse toward your brother's wife.

precepts.text: The Sadducees put to Christ the case of seven brethren who under this law took one wife.
precepts.point: The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
The Sadducees, which say that there is no resurrection, put this very law to Christ: “Master, Moses said, If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother.” They gave the case of seven brethren who under this law took one wife, the first dying without issue and leaving his wife unto his brother, “Likewise the second also, and the third, unto the seventh”, and asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection, for they all had her.

“Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.” The duty of the husband's brother was for a name in Israel and the land inheritance; in the resurrection there is no marrying at all.

precepts.text: I remember that which Amalek did to Israel; now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have.
precepts.point: At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
“Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt”, and blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. Israel was later commanded through Samuel to repay it: “Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.”

The Lord remembered what Amalek did, laying wait in the way when Israel came up from Egypt and smiting the hindmost, the feeble, the faint and weary. Once Israel had rest from their enemies round about, the remembrance of Amalek was to be blotted out, and here is the command to do it: utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not.

precepts.text: Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim.
precepts.point: At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why: “Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim.” That is what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt. At Rephidim Amalek first came and fought with Israel, meeting them by the way and smiting the hindmost, all that were feeble behind, when Israel was faint and weary; and he feared not God. Remember it, and forget it not.

precepts.text: Write this for a memorial in a book, for the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
precepts.point: At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
At Rephidim, after Amalek first fought with Israel, “the Lord said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.” That is the same word as blotting out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; it was written in a book for a memorial so it would not be forgotten.

“And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it JEHOVAH–nissi: For he said, Because the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.” The Lord hath sworn it, from generation to generation, and that war is still going on even to this day.

precepts.text: The wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger; her husband's brother shall take her to wife, and the firstborn shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead.
precepts.point: Behind the words the wife of the dead stands the law of the husband's brother: if brethren dwell together and one dies having no child, his brother takes the widow to wife, and the firstborn she bears succeeds in the name of the dead brother, that his name be not put out of Israel. That first child is basically the dead brother's child; he gets the rights of inheritance as if the brother were still alive, so the brother's name stays in the earth and his house is built up.

note.label: Ruth 1: Naomi and Ruth Return from Moab

precepts.why:
The law of the husband's brother stands behind the wife of the dead. “If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband’s brother unto her.”

“And it shall be, that the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.” That first child is basically the dead brother's child. He gets the rights of inheritance as if the brother were still alive, so the brother's name stays in the earth and his house is built up.

We are not under that law anymore; we do not have that land inheritance in captivity. It is wicked to pull that scripture today to try to get with your brother's wife after he passes away. Do not be looking at your brother's wife.

note.label: Ruth 1: Naomi and Ruth Return from Moab

precepts.why:
If the brother refused his duty, the law shamed him for it. “And if the man like not to take his brother’s wife, then let his brother’s wife go up to the gate unto the elders, and say, My husband’s brother refuseth to raise up unto his brother a name in Israel, he will not perform the duty of my husband’s brother.”

The elders would call him and speak to him, and if he stood to it and said “I like not to take her”, then his brother's wife would come to him before the elders, “and loose his shoe from off his foot, and spit in his face, and shall answer and say, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother’s house. And his name shall be called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.”

Keeping the name going was the whole purpose of the law. A man who would not build up his brother's house carried that shame on his own name in Israel.

precepts.point: What law is that going back to? This law was taught in full when it was read ahead at Ruth 1:6-9 in these notes: the firstborn carries the weight of the name, and the shoe was loosed from him that would not build up his brother's house.

note.label: Ruth 4: Boaz Redeems the Inheritance

precepts.why:
Whoever took the land had to take the dead brother's wife with it; Ruth the Moabitess came along as a parcel of the land, to keep the name of Mahlon alive. That goes back to the duty of the husband's brother. “If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband’s brother unto her.”

“And it shall be, that the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.” That is what Boaz means by raising up the name of the dead upon his inheritance.

Notice the bottom of verse 5: upon his inheritance. This law applies to inheritance; it went into the law of land being passed down. It does not apply today. Your husband dying does not mean his brother now has to go in unto you and raise up children, because that duty was due to the law of inheritance, and Israel has no land inheritance in this captivity. It is wicked to pull that scripture today to try to get with your brother's widow.

precepts.why:
The law also dealt with the brother who refused. “And if the man like not to take his brother’s wife, then let his brother’s wife go up to the gate unto the elders, and say, My husband’s brother refuseth to raise up unto his brother a name in Israel, he will not perform the duty of my husband’s brother.”

If he stood to it before the elders, his brother's wife would “loose his shoe from off his foot, and spit in his face, and shall answer and say, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother’s house. And his name shall be called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.”

The shoe was loosed from him that would not build up his brother's house. That is the weight behind Boaz telling the kinsman that whoever buys the field must also take Ruth, the wife of the dead: the name of Mahlon had to be raised up upon his inheritance.

precepts.text: The loosed shoe was the testimony in Israel against him that would not build up his brother's house; his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.
precepts.point: You can read about that shoe back in Deuteronomy 25.

note.label: Ruth 4: Boaz Redeems the Inheritance

precepts.why:
The kinsman drew off his shoe, and that was the manner in former time in Israel, a testimony to confirm all things. You can read about that shoe back in Deuteronomy 25. “Then shall his brother’s wife come unto him in the presence of the elders, and loose his shoe from off his foot, and spit in his face, and shall answer and say, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother’s house.”

“And his name shall be called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.” The loosed shoe was the testimony in Israel against him that would not build up his brother's house. So when the kinsman told Boaz, Buy it for thee, and drew off his shoe, he was confirming before all that he gave up the redeeming to Boaz.

precepts.text: Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, how he met thee and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God; the detail is written to stir you up: they preyed on the weak and the tired.
precepts.point: Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows Leviticus 19:18 applies to the children of thy people.

note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt.” Generations after the wilderness, the Most High still remembers, and he told Israel to remember too: “Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt; How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.”

The detail is written to stir you up. They preyed on the weak and the tired.

precepts.text: When the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it. Israel now had rest and a king; the time had come.
precepts.point: Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows Leviticus 19:18 applies to the children of thy people.

note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
The same law told Israel when to act: “Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.” Israel now had rest and a king; the time had come. The generation of Amalekites had returned, and it was time to fulfil what was written.

So the order to Saul is specific: “Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.” Kill all of them, spare none.

The Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness. That answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers.

precepts.text: This is the law concerning Amalek that Samuel was referencing: Israel was commanded to blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven, and Saul did not do it.
precepts.point: The reason is stated plainly: because Saul obeyed not the voice of the Lord, nor executed his fierce wrath upon Amalek. The Most High gave a law concerning Amalek, and Saul did not carry it out; that history was read earlier in this book.

note.label: 1 Samuel 28: Saul and the Woman with the Familiar Spirit

precepts.why:
“Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt; How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.” So Israel was commanded, “thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.”

This is the law concerning Amalek that Samuel was referencing, and Saul did not do it. Samuel said it plainly: “Because thou obeyedst not the voice of the Lord, nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek, therefore hath the Lord done this thing unto thee this day.” That history was read earlier in this book.

So the Lord “is departed from thee, and is become thine enemy”, and he did to Saul exactly as he spake by Samuel: “the Lord hath rent the kingdom out of thine hand, and given it to thy neighbour, even to David.”

precepts.text: The law they were standing on: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her.
precepts.point: This is not saying there is no marriage in the kingdom. It answers the law they built the question on, which will not need to be kept when there is no more dying.

note.label: Matthew 22: The Marriage of the King's Son and the Great Commandment

precepts.why:
The Sadducees, “which say that there is no resurrection”, built their question on this law: “If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband’s brother unto her.”

That is the law they were standing on when they said, “Moses said, If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother.” They stacked up seven brethren and one wife to make the resurrection look absurd: “whose wife shall she be of the seven?”

Christ answered, “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.” In the resurrection “they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.” That is not saying there is no marriage in the kingdom. It answers the law of the husband's brother, a law given because men die and leave no child. When there is no more dying, that law will not need to be kept, and the Sadducees' riddle falls apart.

precepts.text: The levirate law they quoted: a dead man's brother must marry the widow and raise up seed, so the dead man's name is not put out of Israel.
precepts.point: The Sadducees did not even believe in the resurrection, yet they used scriptures they did not believe to try to confound Christ, the same way Christians and five-percenters take our scriptures they reject and use them to try to confound us.

note.label: Acts 4: The Stone the Builders Rejected

precepts.why:
This is the law the Sadducees quoted: “If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband’s brother unto her.”

A dead man's brother must marry the widow and raise up seed, so that the dead man's name is not put out of Israel. The Sadducees knew the law well enough to build a riddle on it, and did not believe the resurrection it was put to.
